title: Fine-tuning Behavioral Cloning Policies with Preference‑Based Reinforcement Learning
claim: Limited offline data yields a confidence set that restricts the policy space, so online preference learning only explores within it.
layout: 2 labeled stages, left-to-right, dotted arrow linking offline set to online loop
description: A two-stage diagram with teal on the left and purple on the right. The left stage is titled 'Offline Estimation'. It shows a large ellipse for trajectory distribution space P(T), with a teal circle of radius R inside it that stands for the Hellinger ball. A teal arrow maps this circle to a second ellipse for policy space Π. Inside Π sits a blob-shaped confidence set Π^offline, with the optimal policy π* marked by a dot. A dotted black arrow leads to the right stage, 'Online Preference Learning'. There, the same blob contains π*. Two purple curved arrows, π¹ and π², leave the blob and point to a purple human icon. Beside the icon is the preference π¹ ≻ π². A caption under the left stage reads 'Hellinger ball around ... in P(T) → confidence set Π^offline in Π'. The eye goes first to the large ellipses and the teal arrow.
caption: Overview of the \bridge{} framework. Offline estimation derives estimators $\bcpolicy$ and $\hat{P}$ using the dataset $\mathbb{D}_n^H$ and constructs a confidence set in trajectory distribution space $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{T})$ as a Hellinger ball (left), which translates to the offline policy confidence set $\Pi^offline$ in policy space $\Pi$ likely to contain $\pi^*$ (middle). The confidence set $\Pi^offline$ is then used to constrain the online preference learning phase (right), where policies are sampled from within this set and presented to the expert for preference feedback.
abstract: Deploying reinforcement learning (RL) in robotics, industry, and health care is blocked by two obstacles: the difficulty of specifying accurate rewards and the risk of unsafe, data-hungry exploration. We address this by proposing a two-stage framework that first learns a safe initial policy from a reward-free dataset of expert demonstrations, then fine-tunes it online using preference-based human feedback. We provide the first principled analysis of this offline-to-online approach and introduce BRIDGE, a unified algorithm that integrates both signals via an uncertainty-weighted objective. We derive regret bounds that shrink with the number of offline demonstrations, explicitly connecting the quantity of offline data to online sample efficiency. We validate BRIDGE in discrete and continuous control MuJoCo environments, showing it achieves lower regret than both standalone behavioral cloning and online preference-based RL. Our work establishes a theoretical foundation for designing more sample-efficient interactive agents.
